source.authors: Gabrielle H. Achtymichuk, Kaitlyn M. Fish, Maud C. O. Ferrari
source.title: The power of concentration: Antipredator responses to diluted frozen crayfish alarm cues provide insights on ecologically relevant concentrations and updates to methodology

method: behavioural bioassay: proportional change in time spent moving after injection of diluted frozen-thawed conspecific alarm cue versus water control; Welch's ANOVA, Games-Howell post hoc
conditions: Wild northern crayfish (Faxonius virilis) from the South Saskatchewan River (summer 2023 for Experiment 2), held individually in 5-L tanks for at least one week before testing; tested indoors at 18 +/- 3 C. Alarm cue made from wild donor crayfish (batches of at least 3, both sexes; five cut sites flushed with water, filtered), stock 1 crayfish per 100 mL, frozen at -20 C for about 1 month and thawed; Experiment 2 diluted the stock 10x, 100x and 1000x with water to 1 crayfish per 1 L, 10 L and 100 L, plus an undiluted 'high' stock and a water control; 20 mL of cue or water was syringe-delivered into a 10-L test tank and the response was the proportional change in time spent moving between 5-min pre- and post-cue periods (video tracked). Methods say n = 20 per treatment, the Figure 2 caption says n = 20-28; N = 126 crayfish across the two experiments. The paper states random assignment to treatment and randomised treatment order, and experimenters blind when setting detection and re-analysing videos. Welch's ANOVA with Games-Howell post hoc; one severe outlier removed from the 1000x group. Dilution series stated by the paper: high, 10x, 100x all reduced activity (high and 10x p<0.001, 100x p=0.004); 1000x did not differ from water (p=0.77), so the response limit lies between the 100x and 1000x dilutions and 100x is the most dilute level that produced a response, not a measured threshold. Behavioural alarm response to a chemical cue of injured conspecifics, not an olfactory-nerve threshold.
quote: Compared to the water control, crayfish had a significant decrease in activity when exposed to the high alarm cue concentration (p<0.001) as well as dilutions of 10x (p<0.001) and 100x (p=0.004), indicative of an antipredator response.
note: Whole Results sentence of 36 words, read intact in three abutting pieces by the page tool (preceding sentence begins 'The mean proportional time spent moving'); the abstract sentence about cues eliciting behaviour 'when diluted in up to 10 L of water' agrees (1 crayfish per 10 L = 100x). Family Cambaridae and order Decapoda as main uses for Cambaridae crayfish (Procambarus clarkii rows); the paper's own taxonomy lines were not read for these ranks. Faxonius is the accepted genus (main's gbif-names.tsv lists Orconectes rusticus as SYNONYM of Faxonius rusticus); Faxonius virilis itself is not in that file. Not on main: git grep of pone.0340001, Faxonius and Orconectes virilis over docs/ and all unit branches finds nothing. source.authors: Andrew P. Nosal, Yi Chao, John D. Farrara, Fei Chai, Philip A. Hastings
source.title: Olfaction Contributes to Pelagic Navigation in a Coastal Shark

method: field tracking of wild sharks with directional hydrophone after release offshore: nares occluded with cotton wool soaked in petroleum jelly (anosmic) versus handled sham controls; track straightness assessed by fractal dimension and Nams' scaling test (CRWdiff)
conditions: Wild leopard sharks caught by handline at a La Jolla, California aggregation site in 2013-2014; 36 sharks overall, of which 11 anosmic and 15 sham controls were released at Site A (11.0 km NW of capture, 550 m bottom depth, 9.1 km from shore) and 10 untreated sharks at Site B (not statistically tested). Sham controls had the nare-plugging handling mimicked with forceps but no cotton inserted. All Site A sharks were mature females; fork length did not differ between groups (values in Table 1, not read). Tracks lasted about 4 h until a transmitter released; manual tracking with Vemco VH110 hydrophone, skiff GPS every 5 min. The paper does not say whether allocation to anosmic or sham was random, nor whether trackers were blind. Sham-control tracks (Abstract, previous sentence) ended 62.6% closer to shore on average with straighter paths significantly directed over scales above 1600 m; anosmic tracks showed no oriented movement beyond the 150 m step size. Release directions did not differ among the three groups (Mardia-Watson-Wheeler W = 5.67, P = 0.23), and anosmic speed did not differ from the theoretical optimum (U = 84, P = 0.13). The results held after current adjustment (Abstract). p-values for the anosmic versus control comparisons are in Table 1 (not read). The measure is navigation (shoreward progress) of the whole animal, not an olfactory detection threshold.
quote: In contrast, tracks of anosmic sharks ended 37.2% closer to shore, following significantly more tortuous paths that approximated correlated random walks.
note: Whole abstract sentence of 22 words, read intact in two abutting pieces on two passes ('In contrast, tracks of anosmic sharks ended 37.2% closer to shore, following significantly more' | 'tortuous paths that approximated correlated random walks.'). The control figure is in the previous sentence and is kept out of the value.
